title: Brief introduction to Ensemble Learning
text:
Ensemble learning is a meta-algorithm technique that combines the predictions of multiple individual models, often called “weak learners,” to produce a single, superior predictive model, or “strong learner.” The fundamental principle is that the collective judgment of diverse models is more accurate and robust than the decision of any single constituent model. By strategically aggregating results, ensemble methods effectively address the core challenges of machine learning: bias, variance, and overfitting, leading to better generalizability on unseen data.




<p>Ensemble methods are typically categorized into three major approaches, distinguished by how the weak learners are trained and how their predictions are combined:</p>


Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating), is a parallel ensemble method primarily aimed at reducing variance and preventing overfitting [1].
Process: Multiple instances of the same base learning algorithm (e.g., decision trees) are trained independently and in parallel. Each model is trained on a different, randomly drawn subset of the original training data using a technique called bootstrap sampling (sampling with replacement).
Aggregation: For classification tasks, predictions are combined using majority voting; for regression tasks, they are combined via averaging.
Key Example: The Random Forest algorithm, which combines bagging with feature randomness (randomly selecting a subset of features for each tree).
Goal: To stabilize high-variance models, making them less sensitive to minor fluctuations in the training data.




Boosting is a sequential ensemble method designed primarily to reduce bias and transform weak learners into a strong learner.

Process: Models are trained sequentially. Each subsequent model focuses specifically on correcting the errors and misclassifications made by the previous model in the sequence. Data points that were incorrectly predicted are given higher weight, forcing the next model to concentrate on those difficult samples.
Aggregation: Predictions are combined using a weighted average, where better-performing models are given higher influence.
Key Examples: AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting) [3], Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM) [4], and the highly optimized derivatives like XGBoost [5], LightGBM, and CatBoost.
Goal: To improve the accuracy of models that are otherwise too simplistic (high bias).




Stacking, also known as Stacked Generalization [2], is a layered ensemble method that focuses on improving predictive accuracy by leveraging model diversity.

Process:

Level-0 Models (Base Models): Multiple diverse base models (e.g., a decision tree, a neural network, and a K-Nearest Neighbors classifier) are trained on the original dataset.
Meta-Model (Level-1 Model): The predictions generated by the Level-0 Models are collected and used as the input features for a final, higher-level model called the meta-learner.

Aggregation: The meta-model learns the optimal way to combine the base models’ predictions, essentially learning their individual strengths and weaknesses.
Goal: To exploit the unique strengths of heterogeneous (different) model types.








Features
Advantage
Disadvantage / Trade-off




Accuracy
Significantly higher predictive accuracy and often the best choice for competitive data science.
Risk of overfitting in sequential methods (Boosting) if not carefully tuned.


Robustness
Increased stability against noisy data and outliers, particularly with Bagging.
Sensitive to noisy data (Boosting may assign high weight to outliers).


Bias/Variance
Explicitly targets and reduces model bias (Boosting) and variance (Bagging).
Selection of base models and proper tuning can be highly complex.


Interpretability
N/A
Low Interpretability: The final combined model is a “black box,” making it hard to explain how specific features drive a prediction.


Complexity
N/A
High Computational Cost: Requires more processing power and time due to training and storing multiple models.







We can find references on many GitHub repositories; particularly the following repositories that often curate resources, papers, and sample code - which can be a great starting point for learning:

yzhao062/awesome-ensemble-learning:

This is an “awesome list” repository that curates a collection of ensemble learning books, academic papers, videos, and toolboxes/libraries. It’s an excellent resource for a comprehensive overview of the field.

gkunapuli/ensemble-methods-notebooks:

A collection of companion Jupyter notebooks for the book Ensemble Methods for Machine Learning. It contains practical, hands-on examples of Bagging, Random Forests, Boosting (AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost), and Stacking.

PacktPublishing/Ensemble-Machine-Learning-Cookbook:

The code repository accompanying the Ensemble Machine Learning Cookbook, providing practical recipes and code for implementing ensemble techniques like averaging, voting, bagging, boosting, and stacking in Python.




Ensemble learning is an indispensable pillar of contemporary machine learning. When high predictive performance is the paramount goal—such as in finance, medical diagnostics, or competitive predictive modeling—ensemble methods like Random Forest and XGBoost are the default solutions. While they sacrifice model interpretability and increase computational overhead, the substantial gains in accuracy and robustness makes them worth the trade-off for complex, real-world problems.




[1] L. Breiman, “Bagging Predictors,” Machine Learning, vol. 24, no. 2, pp. 123-140, 1996.
[2] D. H. Wolpert, “Stacked Generalization,” Neural Networks, vol. 5, no. 2, pp. 241-259, 1992.
[3] Y. Freund and R. E. Schapire, “A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting,” J. Comput. Syst. Sci., vol. 55, no. 1, pp. 119-139, 1997.
[4] J. H. Friedman, “Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine,” Ann. Stat., vol. 29, no. 5, pp. 1189–1232, 2001.
[5] T. Chen and C. Guestrin, “XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System,” in Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 2016.

title: The shift in Research and Learning workflow.
text:
The shift in Research and Learning workflow.

In today’s AI era, the workflow in the learning and research process has improved a lot. Previously, research activities tended to be more onsite, where the research team had to go for field observation, collect and store data to a portable storage device, process data and conduct analysis using stand-alone computer, before it could finally be disseminated. But now, a research group can work separately on different locations. The collected data can be stored and shared, so that it can be processed and analysed by other team members elsewhere. 
Under this collaborative workflow, we probably will have to work more often with the command line (terminal/cmd, powershell, bash, etc.); especially during the authentication process to the network, uploading and downloading the data to be distributed, as well as when working with GIT (version control system). In addition, we will also work more often with the python programming language, considering the many applications to help with research data processing developed with the python language, notably: scikit and R - for statistics, markdown - for writing documentation, various apps for image processing and GIS, etc. 
But don’t worry. Currently, all popular search engines (e.g.: google, or bing) already enhanced with AI features. Moreover, we can do the troubleshooting with gemini or copilot, or any other AI assistants. Thus, we will easily find commands that are ready to be copied and pasted into the terminal, or other tutorials and supporting references in various file formats.
There’s no doubt that the shift in this workflow, will accelerate and increase the efficiency of the learning and research process. Therefore, I recommend to undergraduate students (especially those studying science and technology) to accustomed yourself with this environment.

text:

This page has three main sections:

blog
projects
lesson


Each has it’s own landing page and _metadata.yml file. Additionally the ejs directory contains a small custom listing template for the main landing page.
I agree with Michell’s idea that some older blog posts should not be rendered; rather, they’re sort of put together with images and text.

title: Barrier to entry in collaborative workflow
text:
Barrier to entry in collaborative workflow

We are now in the “Work From Anywhere” era, where we can work remotely with other colleagues and partners across the globe. As a result - of course - we must adjust the way we work, by staying connected to internet.  There are some jobs that can be done through web-based applications. The barrier to entry for these jobs are not too big, because most of us are used to working with computers through the Graphical User Interface (GUI). Meanwhile, as for students, lecturers and researchers, will often work with git, python, r, markdown, machine learning applications, etc - which mostly use the Command Line Interface (CLI) in the process.  To help with this adaptation and learning process, there are several applications with GUIs (e.g.: Visual Studio Code, RStudio, Jupyter Notebook), in which there is a terminal pane - for executing various custom commands. In addition, most people nowadays have a Google account. Thus, python, markdown and r (all at once) can be learned using Google Colab. With Google Colab, we can share notes and source code with our colleagues very easily. In addition, the notebooks resulted from the learning process will be automatically saved in Google Drive.
